q: The letters 'CM' beside the registration number on a Champagne label identify:
opts: A grower who sells wine vinified for him at his cooperative
A cooperative vinifying members' fruit under its own brand
A house that buys most of its grapes from independent growers
A grower who vinifies and sells only fruit from his own vines
exp: CM is coopérative de manipulation. The distractors are the other three codes a candidate must separate: RC (récoltant-coopérateur) is the grower selling co-op-made wine under his own name, NM (négociant-manipulant) is the house buying fruit, RM (récoltant-manipulant) is the estate grower. Two more matter in practice — SR for a société de récoltants, and MA for marque d'acheteur, a buyer's own brand, which tells you nothing at all about who grew or made the wine. The letters are printed small next to the registration number and are the fastest origin check on any Champagne label.

q: Germany's 2021 wine-law reform reorients classification toward:
ans: Geographic origin (the narrower the origin, the higher the claim) — converging on the Romance model
exp: Prädikat terms persist but the pyramid logic is now territorial.

q: 'Château' on a French label legally requires:
accept: wine from that estate's own vines aop
ans: An AOP wine made wholly from grapes grown on the named estate, and vinified on that estate
exp: No actual castle required; 'château' in Vin de France is barred.

exp: Superiore, by contrast, means more alcohol/aging, not better geography.

q: On a US label, 'Reserve' legally guarantees:
exp: Unregulated in the US (and France); binding in Spain and Italy.

accept: winery owns controls vineyards same ava grown made bottled
100% own-controlled fruit within the ava continuous process
ans: 100% from vineyards owned/controlled by the winery, in the same AVA, crushed-to-bottled on premises
exp: The strictest phrase on an American label.

q: Match the term to its country and force of law.
exp: The Advanced exam loves 'which of these words is law?'

q: Alcohol tolerance on a US label for wines over 14% is:
exp: ±1.0% above 14; ±1.5% at 14 or below (within class limits).

q: 'Mis en bouteille à la propriété' versus 'au château/domaine':
accept: propriete can be coop members estate
ans: 'Propriété' extends to co-op members bottling their own fruit; château/domaine implies the named estate
exp: Gradations of the same estate-bottled idea.

q: The EU's 'traditional terms' protection means a non-EU wine may not label as:
accept: chateau clos cru reserve in eu market
protected terms like clos or vintage port
ans: Protected terms (Château, Clos, Cru, Vintage/Port, Classic…) in the EU market without qualifying
exp: Why an Aussie 'Port' became Tawny and 'Sherry' became Apera at home too.

q: Grand Cru in Saint-Émilion attaches to what, unlike Burgundy?
ans: The estate/château (revisable classification) — not a fixed vineyard site
exp: And plain 'Saint-Émilion Grand Cru' is merely an appellation tier — the exam's favorite French trap.

q: Vintage labeling in the EU requires what minimum from the stated year?
'Sur lie' on a Muscadet label legally implies:
accept: bottled off its lees by set date one winter
aged on lees until bottling within rules
ans: The wine wintered on its fine lees and was bottled off them within the regulated window
exp: Texture and faint CO2 prickle are the sensory markers.

q: Organic wine in the US versus 'made with organic grapes' differs on:
accept: added sulfites prohibited for organic wine
no added so2 for usda organic wine
ans: USDA Organic Wine permits no added sulfites; 'made with organic grapes' allows up to 100 ppm
exp: The EU's organic wine allows modest SO2 — transatlantic confusion guaranteed.

q: IGP replaced which older French designation?
exp: And AOC became AOP in EU-speak; France keeps both acronyms alive.

q: Describe the Cru Bourgeois du Médoc classification as it has worked since its 2020 relaunch.
accept: three tiers of cru bourgeois revalidated every five years
cru bourgeois superieur and exceptionnel awarded on a five year cycle
tiered classification with an audit and a five year expiry
three levels that expire and must be re-earned
ans: Three tiers — Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur and Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel — awarded to the château on blind tasting plus an audit of production, traceability and environmental practice, and revalidated on a five-year cycle instead of held for life
exp: The history explains the design. The 2003 classification was annulled by the French courts in 2007 as procedurally unfair to the excluded; from 2010 to 2018 the name survived only as an annual selection of individual wines, not of estates. The 2020 return to a classification of estates works precisely because it expires — a ranking that must be re-earned is far harder to sue over than one held in perpetuity. Contrast 1855, which has never expired and has been altered once.
